3232.heavy: Three structural grades 'determined by the presence or absence of length and semi-vowels': light = 'short vowels not followed by a semi-vowel'; heavy = 'short vowels followed by a semi-vowel (which may be a member of the next syllable)'; extra heavy = 'long vowels' (pp. 40-41). 3232.dflt: initial: the first syllable following the plus (or hyphen) juncture, also when both syllables are of equal grade (e.g. [kírim] 'cat, obj. case', light-light; [bé·lè·s] 'it could be', extra heavy-extra heavy, p. 43) or the first is heavier ([máyum] 'feet, obj.', heavy-light) and when a heavier syllable is third or later (only secondary stress there)
3232.prule: Within the phonemic word (the stretch bounded by plus juncture /+/, coterminous with informant citation words) there is exactly one prominent syllable of higher pitch and primary stress; it is 'always the first syllable following the juncture unless the second syllable is heavier in which case the second syllable is stressed' (p. 41). Weight is a three-grade scale: light = short vowel not followed by a semi-vowel; heavy = short vowel followed by a semi-vowel; extra heavy = long vowel. Examples p. 41: [cíyel] 'one to be squashed', [ciyí·ya] 'to be all squashed up', [ciyé·da] 'I squashed them up'. A word-internal hyphen juncture /-/ (after a few prefixes, within a few compounds) restarts the computation from the hyphen. Stress is non-phonemic, 'never functional' (p. 27).
3232.srule: Secondary stress is non-rhythmic and weight-driven: every heavy or extra-heavy syllable (short vowel + semivowel, or long vowel) after the primary-stressed syllable carries a secondary stress, proportionately stronger the further it is from the primary; light post-tonic syllables are unstressed (p. 42; table pp. 43-44: S:S: [be:le:s] 'it could be' 1st+2nd, ssS:s [werlebo:sken] 'you will have to come' 1st+3rd, sssS: [kenehale:s] 'it might be' 1st+4th, S:sS: [tu:nuna:] 'to haul big things' 1st+3rd). In words with an internal hyphen juncture /-/ the pre-hyphen part takes only secondary stress, on its first syllable unless its second is heavier (p. 45; [netnen] /+net-nen+/ 'my mother', [wayhola] /+way-hola+/ 'ceremonial pipe', [puba:npurun] /+puba.n-purun+/ 'of those others', p. 46).

3236.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the (morphological) word, quantity-insensitive and non-phonemic; the default/dominant pattern for phonological words and for inflected verbs, where subject and applicative prefixes are inside the stress domain and the object enclitic =i is outside it ([bu.ˈam.pi] 'you ate (something)', [im.ˈpe.ra.ni] 'I use (it) to cut it'). Stressed vowels are realized long with higher intensity (Praat measurements, Figs 2.1-2.4, Table 2.3).
3236.srule: Secondary (less prominent) stress on the second syllable before the penultimate primary, stated for polysyllabic compound words ([ˌma.rja.ˈra:.ro] 'river', [ˌta.ra.ˈkam.rěj] 'ear', p. 49); the author's transcriptions also mark it, alternating leftward from the penult, on other 4-6-syllable words ([ˌmăng.kŏ.ˈke:.i] 'chicken', [ăm.ˌpě.ră.ˈro:.i] 'house lizard', [ˌpĭ.hă.ˌmă.tă.ˈpa:.pu] 'frog', pp. 32-33). tn.translation: INC takes a tonal value opposite to that of the tone it follows. Odienné Dioula is a language with two phonological tones (see Braconnier 1983a and b): INC will thus consist of a high tone after a low tone and a low tone after a high tone. 3241.heavy: long vowels: 'stress is attracted to long vowels'; 'primary stress may be moved to a long vowel not in penultimate position'; trisyllables 'with a long vowel in the final syllable may show stress on that syllable'; 'Metre in these longer words is, however, very sensitive to vowel length'; p. 103 'Primary stress is preferentially placed on a penultimate syllable and upon a long vowel.' 3241.dflt: 2 syllables: penult; 3 syllables: initial (antepenult) in most words; 4 syllables: penult (trochaic dimeter, primary in second foot), a few initial; 5 syllables: primary 'always on the second foot' (penult in dactyl-trochee, the commonest; antepenult in trochee-dactyl); 6 syllables: commonest trochaic trimeter with primary in the third foot (penult), sometimes 'moved to the second foot' (syllable 3), dactylic dimeter with primary on syllable 4; 7+ syllables: primary stress is normally medial rather than penultimate in the source's examples: syllable 3 of 7 (kà.wa | rréen.da.rla | nàng.ka, 'very common'), syllable 4 of 7 (nyìm.barr.burr | ká.rla | ngù.rru), syllable 3 of 8 (kà.wa | rrám.nya | mà.nga | nàng.ka), syllable 4 of 9 (kà.wa.rra | máa.li | mà.rla | nàng.ka), syllable 5 of 10 (kà.wa | rràm.nya | máa.li | mà.rla | nàng.ka), with secondary stresses on the remaining feet from the first syllable; the last foot takes primary only when -(y)eerri is word-final or in kinship nominals in -nangkáya/-nangkórri. The author gives no quantity-insensitive formula for these long polymorphemic verbs; primary sits on or near the root, which the source does not state as a rule ('there is a tendency, although not a particularly strong one, for metrical foot boundaries to be correlated with morphology').
3241.prule: Primary stress is attracted to the penultimate syllable and to long vowels, with 'quite a bit of variability' and global (rhetorical) stress overriding local placement; stress is not phonemic. By length: bisyllables penult 'almost absolutely, regardless of length variations' (trochee); trisyllables mostly initial (dactyl), final if the final vowel is long (anapaest), penult if the penult vowel is long or the word is lexically specified (amphibrach), some words ambivalent; four syllables: commonest trochaic dimeter with primary in the second foot (penult), a few with primary in the first foot, final if the final vowel is long, iambic dimeter (primary on syllable 2) with long vowels in even syllables; five syllables: 'Primary stress is always on the second foot' (penult in the commonest dactyl-trochee, antepenult in trochee-dactyl); six syllables: commonest trochaic trimeter with primary in the third foot (penult), sometimes 'moved to the second foot' (syllable 3), and 'another important' dactylic dimeter with primary in the second foot (syllable 4, antepenult); seven or more syllables: primary stress is typically MEDIAL, not penultimate: 'A trochee-dactyl-trochee pattern with primary stress on the second foot is very common in seven-syllable words, but with primary stress moved to the third foot when the final morpheme is -(y)eerri' (kà.wa | rréen.da.rla | nàng.ka, primary on syllable 3 of 7; other seven-syllable patterns put primary on syllable 4, or on the penult in kinship nominals ending -nangkáya/-nangkórri); eight-syllable trochaic tetrameter with primary in the second of four feet (kà.wa | rrám.nya | mà.nga | nàng.ka), nine-syllable primary on syllable 4, ten-syllable trochaic pentameter with primary in the third of five feet, the following feet carrying secondary stress; 'In longer words, metrical patterns usually become somewhat more predictable, often with trochaic meter in words with an even number of syllables, and a mixture of trochaic and dactylic feet in words with an odd number of syllables'; primary moves to the last foot when -(y)eerri is final ('again with primary stress attracted to the PROGRESSIVE morpheme -(y)eerri if present'). 'Metre in these longer words is, however, very sensitive to vowel length, and may be completely altered by the occurrence of long vowels in a word.'
3241.srule: Secondary stress (grave accent in the source) falls on the heads of the non-primary feet: predominantly the first syllable and alternate syllables thereafter, in trochaic metre (even-syllabled words) or trochaic metre with a dactyl (odd-syllabled words), on both sides of the primary in long words (e.g. kà.wa|rrám.nya|mà.nga|nàng.ka, 8 syllables); a long antepenultimate vowel may take secondary stress before a primary-stressed penult (ku.ngè|ngá.nu); sub-dominant iambic/anapaestic parses stress even syllables; placement varies with vowel length and 'The difference between primary and secondary stress is not rigidly maintained'.

3243.prule: Accent falls on the stem-initial (radical) syllable of the noun, i.e. the first syllable after the noun-class prefix; the prefix and every post-initial stem syllable are unaccented. Correlates named by the source: the accented syllable is never realised Low, is the only syllable that may carry a contour tone (HB or BH), and the only one with a lengthened vowel. Tone (H vs B) remains lexically distinctive on stems; the accent conditions tonal rules (contour reduction on prefixes, H-spreading blocked by a long radical vowel). Position is set by morphological structure (stem vs prefix), not by the word edge or syllable count.

3244.heavy: No weight rule is stated. Hedged observation on the minority of trisyllables with penult stress: 'Most of this latter category have an open first syllable with a short vowel, and a second closed or long vowel syllable' (i.e. a CVC or CVV second syllable), immediately qualified: 'It is possible that either 1)the prefix is not normally stressed or 2) that the relative length of the stem vowel in comparison to the short vowel of the prefix is perceived as stress by this listener.' Also 'there may be some difference between open and closed syllable prefixes in attracting stress'. Fn. 21: 'The relationship between vowel length and stress patterns needs further investigation.'
3244.dflt: Count-dependent edge stress as in: initial in 2-4 syllable monomorphemic words, penult (with initial secondary) in 5-syllable words; the author's headline for words over 3 syllables is penult.
3244.prule: Count-dependent, quantity-insensitive edge stress stated per word length: 2 syllables initial ('gaabu, 'wiila); 3 syllables 'normally' initial = antepenult ('wundugu, 'pajaja), a minority penult (gu'raarra, bu'gaya, bi'yangga); 4-syllable mono-morphemic and reduplicated words primary initial + secondary penult ('wara,warta, 'bundu,wali); 5 syllables primary penult + secondary initial, dactyl + trochee (wanawa'narra,nyarrmira'nerri); 6-syllable reduplications primary on the first syllable of the second copy = antepenult (burrundi'burrundi,wamarlu'marlurlu). The author's own headline generalisation is 'In words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable.' NOTE (C): the 4-syllable cell is internally contested in the source: the dedicated paragraph and its three examples ('wara,warta, 'bundu,wali, 'lewa,rlewa) give primary initial for mono-morphemic and reduplicated words, while the headline 'more than 3 syllables... penultimate' would give penult; the grid follows the explicit per-length statement, and polymorphemic 4-syllable words are not fixed by the source ('nguma'ngarri on p. 63 carries two primary marks).
3244.srule: Secondary stress at the word edge opposite the primary: on the first syllable when primary is penultimate (words of more than three syllables, e.g.,wanawa'narra; 6-syllable reduplications,burrundi'burrundi), on the third = penultimate syllable when primary is initial (4-syllable mono-morphemic and reduplicated words, 'wara,warta); some trisyllables may carry final secondary stress ('murdu,ra); monosyllabic postpositions after disyllabic hosts often add word-final secondary stress ('yawal,-gu).
3244.quote: In words of more than 3 syllables primary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress on the first syllable. 3246.prule: No placement rule stated. The source says Wyandot has primary word accent; reflexes of PNI long vowels (merged with short vowels in Wyandot) 'have acquired primary word accent'; 'many, but not all' words whose final syllable had a PNI long vowel carry final accent (teˈnih 'two', ahˈsɛ̃h 'ten', jaˈʒuɁ 'animal', jatuːˈjɛ̃h 'it is certain', wɛ̃ːˈnat 'Wyandot'); the other cited Wyandot forms carry penultimate or antepenultimate accent (jaˈnɔ̃hʃaɁ 'house', uˈnaɁtaɹaɁ 'bread', unrahˈtaɁjeh 'on the leaves', ˈtsiɁnwaɹaɁ 'green', hahˈʃɹɔ̃njah 'he makes it') but no default rule is written; the author calls the accent patterns 'unexpected' and defers their analysis.
3246.srule: Exists in the transcription record but placement not described: Barbeau's Wyandot phonetic key marks 'minor or secondary stress' (grave) as distinct from the main stress (acute) on words in his 1911-12 texts, with no rule for where it falls (Barbeau 1915:27; 1960:57-58); Julian 2010 (source of the primary statement) does not mention secondary stress; no analysis found (Kopris 2014:98 notes only that Barbeau's primary and secondary marks are mutually exclusive).

3248.dq: As a general rule, the accent in Kaffir is put upon the penult, that is, the last syllable but one, as bámba, ubúso, andibóni. When a word is lengthened by inflexion at the end, the accent is moved forward so as to remain on the penult, as bambáni, ebuswéni, andibonánga.

3248.prule: Accent (realized as syllable length, p. 2) on the penultimate syllable of the word; when suffixes lengthen the word or a monosyllabic enclitic (-ke, -na, -nye, -mzi) is joined, the accent moves so as to remain penultimate in the enlarged unit.
3248.srule: Long derivative words have a secondary accent on the syllable that would be the penult of the simple word they are derived from (umtételéli < teta, uménzeleléli < énza); compound words also have a secondary accent on the penult of their first member (umtételiwáka, hlángabéza). Placement morphological (base / first-member penult), not rhythmic.

3248.tone: McLaren 1906 marks no tone and calls the penult prominence 'accent'. Xhosa is a two-tone (H vs toneless) language with no lexical vowel-length contrast; the modern first-hand sources held describe the same prominence as automatic penultimate lengthening independent of H-tone placement: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1997 ROA-176 'In Isixhosa, the penult syllable of a Prosodic Word in phrase-final position is lengthened and considered prominent' (H tones shift to the antepenult, 'Avoid Prominence') 'automatic lengthening that affects the penultimate syllable of a word that stands in utterance-final position'; Jokweni 1994 (no vowel length contrast, long penult derived by rule); Bloom Ström 2022 (utterance-penult ~217 ms in declaratives, reduced in questions). Downing 2004 codes Nguni as penult stress-accent with tone (Doke 1954). Dissent on the label: Jordan 1956 UCT PhD vol. 1 secs 2.113-2.121 (typed pp. 115-121) gives the same penult LENGTH facts ('The penultimate syllable of a sense-group is normally long... If an extra syllable is added at the end length shifts to the new penultimate syllable') but holds that 'this widely-accepted view [main stress on the penult] is mistaken': 'In ordinary speech stress is seldom prominent', and emphatic stress falls on the root syllable irrespective of position.

3249.tone: Changsha Xiang has six lexical tones, all contour tones (p. 3, Table 1). The source does not posit a stress phoneme; 'metrical stress' is diagnosed from tone sandhi and duration in 180 disyllabic compounds x 5 speakers: σ1 longer [F(1,1798)=2033, p<.001], ratio 1.53 (SD 0.48), keeps its citation contour; σ2 shortened, surface tone levelled to [33]/[44]; foot given as (s w) (p. 15, ex. 4). 3250.prule: Stem-final: stress falls on the last syllable of the radical (stem); the nominal (nuclear-case) suffix -a lies outside the domain, so -a-final nouns surface penultimate ('a.ka 'casa' < 'ak+a) while stem-final words are oxytone (ka'ʔi 'macaco'). Compounds: primary stress on the stressed syllable of the last member.

3252.dq: Stress (ˈa) is a phoneme of its own. [contrasted with the sentence-level statement:] Sentence questions are distinguished from statements only by a rising tone and stress on the last syllable
3252.dloc: §2.13 'Tone and stress', p. 35 (PDF spread 5 of 18 = pp. 34-35); §2.6 'The question', p. 60 (spread 18 = pp. 60-61).
3252.prule: Stress is phonemic (contrastive): Heine lists it as a phoneme of its own, marked per word with ˈ before the stressed vowel, alongside distinctive tone; no positional, weight or morphological rule for its placement is stated anywhere in the sketch. In the data stress falls in varying positions (e.g. ˈiíçeʼ 'I', nawˈáxan 'see', wˈaaʼ 'cows', p. 36). The only positional statement is sentence-level: yes/no questions take rising tone and stress on the sentence-final syllable.
3252.srule: Not mentioned in Heine 1974/75 (§2.1 Phonology incl. §2.13 'Tone and stress' p. 35, §2.6 p. 60, examples pp. 36-60, and Part 2 §3 Vocabulary pp. 119-138 checked): the sketch's whole word-stress statement is 'Stress (ˈa) is a phoneme of its own', and the data carry one stress mark per word.
3252.quote: 2.13. Tone and stress. There are at least two distinctive tones: high (marked by an accent aigu, e.g. á) and low (left unmarked). Furthermore, mid (ā), falling (â) and rising tone (ǎ) will be marked, although it is not known whether they are distinct units. Stress (ˈa) is a phoneme of its own. [p. 60, §2.6] Sentence questions are distinguished from statements only by a rising tone and stress on the last syllable, e.g. ísí alɛ'ɛ 'he is coming': ísí alɛ'ˈɛ̌ 'is he coming?'; damatú alɛ'ɛ́to 'the woman is coming': damatú alɛ'ɛ́tˈǒ 'is the woman coming?'

Question intonation = rising tone plus stress on the final syllable.

3253.tone: OPD p.3: 'Tone is phonemic but has a low functional load' with two word-level minimal pairs; p.4: 'Tone is not written.' The heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' is the OPD template rubric, not a claim that stress or length were analysed; nothing on stress anywhere in the 4 pages (the only other prosody-adjacent line is 'Nasals and lateral [l] can be syllabic, especially word initially before a plosive'). The two pairs each carry one acute per word, which would be consistent with a lexical pitch accent, but the source calls it tone and gives no culminativity or placement analysis. Lloyd 1973: 87 (family level, not Yagwoia-specific): 'Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem. Angaataha, with four tonemes, is noticeably different from the other Angan languages. In Angaataha stress is also linked to high tone. Thus Angaataha is like a "tone language" and the others are more "intonation languages"'; also 'Vowels tend to be slightly longer in stressed syllables or in short words, then in unstressed syllables or in long words.' Lloyd's Yagwoia phonology section (pp. 53-55, from Weier & Grieger 1960) covers 13 consonants, 7 vowels, allophony and clusters and says nothing about stress or tone.

3255.dq: Word stress is phonemic. [...] The majority of words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Some stress falls on the final. But, the stress remains in its original position, even when plural or other suffixes are added.
3255.dloc: Section PHONOLOGY, p.469 and p.471; noun-list note p.474. Acute accents verified (drops them).
3255.prule: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive). Two patterns: the majority of words are stressed on the penultimate syllable, a lexical minority on the final syllable; nine minimal pairs of segmentally identical disyllables (ai 'tree': aí 'foot', mata 'to die': matá 'an eye', utu 'louse': utú 'happiness'...). Stress is a property of the stem and stays in its original position when plural or possessive suffixes are added (u-ái 'my tree': aí-u 'my foot'; si ána 'they shoot an arrow': si aná 'their child'). The author calls it 'an unpredictable stress pattern' and 'phonemic stress'.

3258.heavy: A word-final long vowel: the 1st-person marker /-ː/ in most Central varieties ('la vocal larga que funciona como marcador de primera persona se acentúa cuando está en posición final de palabra'); in Huallaga and some other varieties also final long vowels of other origin. A final closed syllable is explicitly not treated like a final long vowel ('no trata a las palabras que terminan en vocal larga como a las que terminan en consonante').
3258.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable; a word-final long vowel is stressed instead (in 'most Central varieties' the 1st-person marker /-ː/; in Huallaga 'and some other varieties' any final long vowel, e.g. /-raq/ realised [-ráː]). Equivalently, under the V=VV analysis, 'stress the penultimate vowel' (penultimate mora). Final closed syllables do not attract stress.
